content.p: On the morning of 9 September 1924, about 40 Kauai sheriffs, deputies and recently deputized hunters went to a strike camp in the village of Hanapepe to bring out two Filipino sugar workers who were said to be held there against their will. Within minutes, 16 striking Filipino workers and four police officers were dead. Many more were wounded, and more than 100 strikers were arrested. Nobody has established who made the first move. A shot, or a loud noise that may not have been a shot, set off the fighting, and researchers now trying to reconstruct it say the accounts that survive favour the winning side.

The event is called both the Hanapepe Massacre and the Battle of Hanapepe. A century later it is commemorated by the State of Hawaii, whose Department of Accounting and General Services calls it a foundational and tragic episode in the history of workers' rights.
content.h2: The last to arrive, the first to be evicted
content.p: Filipinos were the last group of immigrant laborers brought to Hawaii's sugar plantations. Honolulu Magazine counts 37,019 who came between 1907 and 1924. On Kauai they worked and lived on the Koloa, Makaweli, Kekaha, Lihue and McBryde plantations, in the worst housing and at the lowest-paid jobs. Most were young, single men, and they came from three regions of the Philippines. Visayans arrived first, then Ilocanos, then, in much smaller numbers, Tagalogs. Each group spoke a different language. Filipino laborers earned roughly $20 to $25 a month, the magazine reports, and sent much of what remained to relatives at home.

Japanese workers had struck first, in 1909, and in 1920 the Federation of Japanese Labor led a large strike on Oahu in which Filipino workers, led by the organiser Pablo Manlapit, also took part. According to the Hawaii Division of the ILWU, Manlapit arrived as a laborer in 1910, was dismissed from a Big Island plantation three years later after he and other workers protested a pay cut, and was then put on a list of troublemakers circulated to plantation managers. He worked in Honolulu as a janitor and an interpreter for a lawyer, taught himself law, and in 1919 became the first Filipino licensed to practice law in Hawaii.

The Higher Wage Movement was launched in 1922 by Manlapit together with George Wright, who worked at Pearl Harbor and was connected to the American Federation of Labor. It asked for a minimum of $2 a day where most Filipino workers earned $1 for ten hours, and for an eight-hour day. Honolulu Magazine adds overtime pay, equal pay for women and men, and collective bargaining to the list. In April 1923 they sent the Hawaiian Sugar Planters' Association petitions signed by 6,000 Filipino workers. The association ignored them, according to the ILWU.

Striking was almost the only legal option left. The ILWU's account of the period says that picketing was illegal, that interfering with a business in any way was illegal, and that any two or more workers could be arrested for unlawful assembly. A worker who stopped work lost his plantation housing. That, it says, is why the Visayan strikers on Kauai ended up camped in a Japanese-language school and a banana patch at Hanapepe.
content.h2: A strike that barely took hold on Kauai
content.p: The strike began in 1924 on Oahu and spread to the Big Island, to Maui and, a few months later, to Kauai. Scholars quoted by Honolulu Magazine are blunt about its organisation. The linguist John Reinecke wrote that "No other major strike was so haphazardly planned and conducted or failed so completely". Jon Okamura, a University of Hawai'i professor of ethnic studies, said that Manlapit's union, unlike the Japanese one, had no branches at plantation level.

Kauai was where the strike was weakest. Filipinos made up about half of the island's plantation workforce, 5,576 people, and an estimated 575 struck. The historian Andy Bushnell explains that before the stoppage a labor commissioner from the Philippines, Cayetano Ligot, visited the island to assure the planters that Filipino workers would not strike, and that he was most successful in persuading Ilocanos. Most of the strikers were Visayans. About 150 of them took over the rented schoolhouse for Japanese-language classes at Hanapepe around the end of July or the start of August; more than 400 others gathered in a rice warehouse in Kapaa. The two towns were chosen because they were not plantation towns controlled by the planters' association.

The strikers had no strike fund. According to a 1979 oral-history project at the University of Hawai'i that Honolulu Magazine draws on, some had families at the camp, fished in the Hanapepe River, and relied on local shopkeepers for food. Chad Taniguchi, who grew up on Kauai's west side, learned that his grandfather, who ran a small bakery in Hanapepe, had donated food. Bushnell described the mood by then as frustrated: the strikers were not shutting anything down, they had little to eat, and the industry went on producing sugar.

On 8 September two Ilocano workers from the Makaweli plantation, each about 18 years old according to Honolulu Magazine, rode into Hanapepe to buy a pair of $4 shoes. On the way back they passed the strike headquarters, where, the magazine says, they were apparently attacked by Visayan strikers and held in the schoolhouse. Sulpicio Venyan, a striker interviewed for the oral-history project, conceded that some strikers beat the two and forced them inside, where they spent the night. Bushnell speculated that they were taken because they were non-striking Ilocanos. The film-maker Stephanie Castillo says newspapers have told the story that way for 95 years, but she calls it the victors' history: in her view little work was done to interview the strikers who went to jail or were deported.

Friends reported the pair missing to the sheriffs. Deputy Sheriff William Crowell visited the headquarters that evening and asked to see them. The strikers produced the two men, who are believed to have been pressured into saying they wanted to be there. Crowell left, obtained from the county attorney an arrest warrant for the two captives, not for any striker, and returned the next morning with about 40 men. Many were hunters who had been deputized as sharpshooters, with weapons and training paid for by the planters' association, Honolulu Magazine says. The ILWU says they carried high-powered rifles and were placed on a hill above the banana patch.

Crowell went to the headquarters with about three officers and an interpreter. The remaining 37 or so stayed at their cars along the road, some on a small hill from which the school was visible in the distance.

What happened next is told in three ways. The official account, given by one of Crowell's officers who was at the school and quoted by Honolulu Magazine, says Crowell showed the warrant, the two men were released, and as they left with him some strikers followed, taunting them and waving cane knives. The sharpshooters, it says, fired when they saw strikers try to attack Crowell. The account describes the 16 deaths as self-defense and says four officers suffered casualties from stab wounds. The ILWU says an official investigation concluded that the Filipinos fired first on the police and then attacked with cane knives. A 1924 Star-Bulletin story, as summarised by the Star-Advertiser in 2019, put 100 to 200 strikers around the deputy sheriff, armed with pistols, knives and clubs.

Venyan gave a different version. Crowell grabbed the two men and started to run, he said, and when strikers chased them "that's when the shooting started. They just started killing the Filipinos." Venyan said he was not part of the violence and ran with others into the banana patch. The ILWU says that as the police were leaving a shot was fired and, in the confusion, police and deputized hunters began shooting the workers; it adds that later interviews with witnesses and survivors suggest the event was more likely a tragic mistake and an overreaction by the police and hunters. Michael Miranda, who led a research team for the Filipino American National Historical Society, said in 2019 that the most consistent account his team had found so far was that the strikers stood accused of abducting or beating two men who had ignored the picket line, and that "a loud noise that may or may not have been gunfire" triggered the fighting. Language barriers and the anti-union climate of the 1920s made it harder for either side to calm things, he said. The Star-Advertiser reported that the gunfire reportedly lasted about five minutes.
Honolulu Magazine puts it plainly: no one knows who made the first move.

Most sources agree on 16 strikers and four police officers dead. Hawaii News Now, citing the county of Kauai, says three of the four officers were of Hawaiian heritage and one was of Chinese descent. A 2024 Spectrum News report on a county event lists the dead as 16 Filipino laborers plus three Hawaiian laborers, one Chinese laborer and four officers, which comes to more than the 20 given everywhere else. Crowell was injured but survived, Honolulu Magazine says.

Honolulu Magazine reports that about 100 strikers, Venyan among them, were rounded up and taken to the prison in Lihue, while the injured and the dead were taken to a nearby hospital. National Guard soldiers arrived on Kauai by inter-island steamer; the ILWU describes them as heavily armed. Funerals were held for the officers and for the strikers separately. The Garden Island newspaper reported that 16 rough board caskets were taken to Hanapepe by truck and placed in one long trench, and the graves were left unmarked. The planters' association gave each of the four officers' families $500; the families of the 16 strikers shared about $75, barely $5 for each dead man, according to the magazine.
content.h2: Prosecutions and the end of the strike
content.p: The numbers on the court cases vary. Spectrum News says more than 100 strikers were arrested. The ILWU says 76 were tried and 60 got four-year prison terms. Honolulu Magazine, relying on Bushnell, says 76 were indicted for rioting and 16 were acquitted, Venyan among them, that two others were charged with assault and battery for beating the Ilocano pair, and that most received four-year sentences, with some deported to the Philippines. The same piece also quotes Bushnell as saying that 57 strikers were given 13 months in jail and went back to work afterwards. The state's Department of Accounting and General Services says 58 strikers pleaded guilty and received four-year sentences. According to Honolulu Magazine nobody was charged with murder, and the Kauai sheriffs were not reprimanded for their part in the violence.

Manlapit was not on Kauai that day, as Michael Miranda of the Kauai Philippine Cultural Center has said, and the ILWU says he had nothing to do with the incident. Honolulu Magazine says he was on trial in Honolulu on conspiracy charges in an unrelated case. The ILWU says he was convicted of conspiracy and imprisoned on Oahu from 1925, then freed two years later on the condition that he leave Hawaii. The ILWU adds that leaders and suspected leaders on other plantations were fired and sent back to the Philippines, and without them the Higher Wage Movement fell apart.

Honolulu Magazine argues that the massacre derailed the Filipino labor movement rather than rallying it. There was no public outcry, it says. Okamura said the violence reinforced an existing stereotype of young Filipino men as violent, and gave Japanese workers a further reason not to cooperate with Filipinos. Because the strikers had been armed and four police had died, he said, the larger public was unlikely to sympathise. After 1924 the ILWU says the planters stopped recruiting Visayans and drew workers from the Ilocos region, rejecting educated recruits, which it reads as a deliberate attempt to keep Filipinos divided. Within a few years Ilocanos were the majority on the plantations.

Plantations did not accept union labor until 1946, when they recognised the International Longshoremen and Warehouse Union, the magazine says; Spectrum News dates effective strikes and unions between 1937 and 1958. Miranda has called the 1924 strike unsuccessful but said it "laid significant groundwork" for workers' rights, and Hawaii News Now says it laid the foundation for the idea of an interracial union.
content.h2: Finding the graves and building a memorial
content.p: The massacre was remembered, in the words of Honolulu Magazine in 2009, mainly through the diligence of a handful of historians. Its relative obscurity, the magazine suggested, came from there being no clear-cut victims or villains, and no real aftereffects of the strike.

A committee organising the Kauai Filipino centennial put up a concrete marker in Hanapepe Town Park, dedicated on 9 September 2006. The Filipino American National Historical Society's Kauai team began researching the event in 2018. Its chairman, Miranda, said in 2019 that the group might never find the true story because those involved had been killed, deported or arrested, and that it hoped to find where the dead strikers lay. A documentary, "The Hanapepe Massacre Mystery," was filmed alongside the search, which was to focus on two areas: one around a small concrete marker inside the Hanapepe Filipino Cemetery that carries no name, only "Born 1886. Died Sept. 9. 1924." (it was not known whether it marked any of the strikers), and one in brush beyond the cemetery's western boundary. In 2019, Spectrum News says, the society worked with a technician and an engineer to find the burial site.

For the centennial in September 2024, the County of Kauai Planning Department held a ceremony attended by nearly 150 people, including officials and descendants. The county was working to buy two parcels near where the fighting began, for which the county council had allocated $1,444,000. Mayor Derek Kawakami told the gathering it was "a story that should never be forgotten".

The state is building a memorial at the front of the cemetery, where the strikers lie in a mass grave. It will be two concrete columns with a gap between them, standing for the two sides of the conflict and angled so that a shadow is always cast. In July 2026 the Department of Accounting and General Services chose Pacific Blue Construction LLC for the work, at $125,000, with construction due to begin on 1 September 2026. A talk on Pablo Manlapit and the massacre was scheduled for 10 September 2026 in Lihue; it was to include a discussion of efforts to secure justice for him.
